implementation_notes: ts-rule-engine brings the pattern into the type system: a rule is a typed object with an id/name, a weight (higher fires first, insertion order on ties), a condition function returning boolean and an action function that receives the fact plus { rule, stop, logger }, so stopping the run is explicit and logging is built in. The engine owns the fact, re-runs rules when an action changed it and enforces a max-iteration guard against non-convergence, which makes the execution model visible instead of implicit. Because rules are functions the rule base ships with the code; the library's value is the ordered, bounded, observable evaluation loop rather than a rule store.
pitfalls: Weights are the only conflict resolution: without them rules run in insertion order, so precedence lives in the array rather than in the rule, and a fact-mutating action can make later rules oscillate until the max-iteration guard trips.
stop() halts the engine but not the mutation: rules that change the fields their own condition reads need explicit guards to stay idempotent.
Rules are TypeScript functions, so the rule base cannot be edited without a rebuild - use it when rules are code, and a JSON engine when they must be data.

variants.name: json-rules-engine with typed facts
variants.idiom_name: json-rules-engine JSON conditions + typed facts and event handlers
variants.implementation_notes: The JSON engine used from JavaScript is the pragmatic TypeScript choice when rules must live outside the bundle: you type the facts object passed to engine.run(), while the condition tree (all/any/not over {fact, operator, value}) stays untyped data that is validated separately. Matches emit events rather than running actions, so the caller maps event types to typed handlers and the engine never mutates facts - which removes the re-trigger problem entirely. Add a runtime schema for the rule JSON (fact names, operators, event params) because TypeScript cannot check it.
pitfalls: TypeScript types the facts passed in, not the fact ids inside the rule JSON: the two drift silently unless the rule store is validated against a schema.
Event types are declared in rule data, so an unknown event is only discovered when the handler map is consulted - make the handler map exhaustive and fail on unknown events.
Facts are read-only inputs to the engine: logic that must change them belongs in the handler, which keeps rules pure but pushes mutation into application code.
